title: Nile cruise prices: why five-star costs €400 or €6,500
standfirst: Two cruises can both call themselves five-star, sail the same route in the same week and differ in price more than 15 times over. The difference is not a mystery: it is the boat, the cabin, the crew, the season and what the price includes. Here we take a price apart.

sections.heading: What a cruise price pays for
paragraphs: Most of a cruise price is the share of running the boat that falls to you: fuel, crew, food, mooring fees and the boat itself, divided by the number of guests. A ship with a hundred and forty guests spreads those costs thinly; a dahabiya with twelve does not.
On top of that come the cabin you choose, how you see the sites (a shared guide or your own Egyptologist), and the season. The breakdown below shows how each one moves the price.

sections.heading: What is never in the price
paragraphs: A Nile cruise runs from check-in on the first day to check-out on the last. Flights, airport transfers and extra tours are separate, and so are crew gratuities, which are expected, paid on board at check-out: usually €5 to €10 per person, per night, depending on the cruise. Check each cruise’s offer.

sections.heading: Comparing like with like
paragraphs: When two prices differ, check four things before anything else: how many guests share the boat, the size of the cabin, how the sightseeing is guided, and the dates. Those four explain most of the gap.

faqs.q: Why is a Nile cruise so cheap on some sites?
faqs.a: The lowest prices are usually for large ships in the hot season, in the smallest cabins, with shared sightseeing. Check what is included and the dates before comparing.

faqs.q: Are prices per person or per cabin?
faqs.a: Per person. Each cruise’s starting price says what it is based on, and when we last checked it. For your dates, ask us to check rates, and we’ll send your offer by email. All prices we publish and quote already include our margin.
